blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 5 (Enzymes), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is metabolism? What regulates it?
blocks.explanation: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical activities occurring in living organisms. It is regulated by enzymes.

book_ref.quote: The sum of all chemical activities occurring in living organisms i.e., metabolism is regulated by enzymes

blocks.prompt: 2 Why is it said that without enzymes there would be no life?
blocks.explanation: Because enzymes speed up reactions enormously (10³ to 10⁸ times). A reaction completed in 30 minutes with an enzyme would take one year without it, which is far too slow for life.

book_ref.quote: Thus, we can say that without enzymes there would have been no life at all

blocks.prompt: 3 Where are enzymes synthesized, and where do they work?
blocks.explanation: All enzymes are synthesized inside cells by ribosomes. Then they either stay and work inside the cell (e.g. glycolysis enzymes dissolved in cytoplasm; protein synthesis enzymes as part of ribosomes) or are secreted out to work at other sites.

book_ref.quote: After their synthesis, either they stay and work inside cell or they are secreted out to work at other sites

blocks.prompt: 4 Why is pepsin produced in an inactive form?
blocks.explanation: Pepsin digests proteins and could destroy the protein-made structures of the cells that make it. So it is produced as inactive pepsinogen, secreted out, and activated to pepsin at its target site.

book_ref.quote: It can destroy protein-made structures present inside cells where it is synthesized

blocks.prompt: 5 Why can only a certain substrate fit into an enzyme's active site?
blocks.explanation: Because the shape of each active site is very specific; it is three-dimensional and bears a specific charge, so only a certain substrate molecule can fit into it.

book_ref.quote: So, only a certain substrate molecule can fit into it

blocks.prompt: 6 Differentiate between binding site and catalytic site.
blocks.explanation: Both are regions of the active site:

book_ref.quote: Catalytic site catalyses the reaction and substrate is transformed into products

rows: Region into which the substrate fits
Region that catalyses the reaction
Holds the substrate by weak forces such as hydrogen bonds
Transforms the substrate into products

blocks.prompt: 7 Differentiate between apoenzyme and holoenzyme.
blocks.explanation: They differ in whether the cofactor is included:

book_ref.quote: The protein part of enzyme is called apoenzyme

rows: The protein part of the enzyme
The complete enzyme
Does not include the cofactor
Includes the cofactor (apoenzyme + cofactor)

blocks.prompt: 8 How do metal ions act as cofactors? Name three such ions.
blocks.explanation: Metal ions such as Ca⁺², Mg⁺², Mn⁺², Cu⁺² and Zn⁺² change the non-functional active sites of enzymes into functional sites. Their attachment changes the shape of the enzyme so it can combine with the substrate.

book_ref.quote: Many enzymes use metal ions, such as Ca⁺², Mg⁺², Mn⁺², Cu⁺², and Zn⁺² as their cofactors

blocks.prompt: 9 How do coenzymes take part in enzyme-catalysed reactions?
blocks.explanation: Coenzymes take part in enzyme-catalysed reactions often by transporting electrons (hydrogen atoms) from one enzyme to another. Many vitamins, e.g. niacin and riboflavin, function as coenzymes.

book_ref.quote: Coenzymes participate in enzyme-catalysed reactions, often by transporting electrons

blocks.prompt: 10 What is the role of NAD⁺ when food is oxidized in a cell?
blocks.explanation: NAD⁺ is a hydrogen acceptor. Enzymes draw electrons from food molecules and transfer them to NAD⁺, which reduces to NADH. NADH carries the energy contained in the electron of the hydrogen atom.

book_ref.quote: The electron of hydrogen atom contains energy that NADH molecule carries

blocks.prompt: 11 Why are trace elements like molybdenum and manganese necessary for health?
blocks.explanation: Because enzymes use trace elements such as molybdenum and manganese as cofactors.

book_ref.quote: which are necessary for our health, are used by enzymes as cofactors

blocks.prompt: 12 How do enzymes lower the activation energy?
blocks.explanation: Enzymes bring reactants together in the correct orientation or stress particular chemical bonds of reactants. So less activation energy is needed for new bonds to form, and the reaction speeds up.

book_ref.quote: Enzymes bring reactants together in correct orientation or stress particular chemical bonds of reactants

blocks.prompt: 13 Do enzymes change the products of a reaction? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: No. Enzymes do not affect the nature or properties of end products. For example, sucrose is always hydrolysed into glucose and fructose whether the enzyme sucrase is present or not; sucrase only speeds it up.

book_ref.quote: The presence of enzymes does not affect the nature or properties of end products

blocks.prompt: 14 What is the ES complex? What happens after it forms?
blocks.explanation: The ES (enzyme-substrate) complex forms when the substrate binds the active site. The catalytic site is activated; its atoms stress and destabilize bonds of the substrate, lowering activation energy, and the substrate is transformed into products. The enzyme then detaches unaltered: E + S → ES → E + P.

book_ref.quote: The atoms of catalytic site stress and destabilize particular bonds of substrate

blocks.prompt: 15 How do enzymes work in a complex metabolic pathway?
blocks.explanation: Many enzymes act in a sequence, present together with their cofactors. The product of one enzyme serves as the substrate of the next, until end products form, which inhibit (through feedback) the first enzyme.

book_ref.quote: In complex metabolic pathways e.g., respiration, photosynthesis, protein synthesis etc.

blocks.prompt: 16 State the lock-and-key model.
blocks.explanation: Proposed by Emil Fischer (1894): as a specific key can open only a specific lock, a specific enzyme can transform only one specific substrate into products. The active site is rigid, with no flexibility before, during or after enzyme action.

book_ref.quote: as a specific key can open only a specific lock

blocks.prompt: 17 Why was the induced fit model proposed?
blocks.explanation: Later studies did not support the lock-and-key model in all reactions. On the basis of new evidence, Daniel Koshland (1958) proposed that the active site is flexible and is modified by substrate binding before catalysis starts.

book_ref.quote: Later studies did not support lock-and-key model in all reactions

blocks.text: 5.4 Factors affecting the rate of enzyme action

blocks.prompt: 18 Name four factors that affect the rate of enzyme action.
blocks.explanation: Temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration.

book_ref.quote: Enzymes are very sensitive to the environment in which they work

blocks.prompt: 19 What is optimum temperature? Give its value for human enzymes.
blocks.explanation: Optimum temperature is the specific temperature at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate. For human enzymes it is 37 °C.

book_ref.quote: Every enzyme works at its maximum rate at a specific temperature called its optimum temperature

blocks.prompt: 20 Why does a rise in temperature up to a certain limit increase the rate of enzyme action?
blocks.explanation: Heat adds to the activation energy, and it gives kinetic energy to substrate and enzyme molecules, so they move rapidly, collide more frequently and the reaction rate increases.

book_ref.quote: When temperature is raised up to a certain limit, the heat adds in activation energy

blocks.prompt: 21 What is denaturation of an enzyme?
blocks.explanation: When temperature rises well above optimum, atomic vibrations become so violent that bonds cannot hold the polypeptide chains in position and the enzyme's globular structure is lost. This is denaturation; the rate falls rapidly and may stop completely.

book_ref.quote: When vibrations become too violent, bonds cannot hold polypeptide chains in the proper position

blocks.prompt: 22 How can thermophilic bacteria live in hot springs?
blocks.explanation: Their proteins have stronger bonding between the polypeptide arms, so their enzymes are not denatured and can function at 70 °C or higher.

book_ref.quote: They have proteins with stronger bonding between their polypeptide arms

blocks.prompt: 23 Differentiate between the pH requirements of pepsin and trypsin.
blocks.explanation: They work best at very different pH:

book_ref.quote: Every enzyme works its best at a specific pH, called its optimum pH

rows: Active in acidic medium (low pH)
Optimum activity in alkaline medium (high pH)
Optimum pH 1.5–1.6
Optimum pH 7.8–8.7

blocks.prompt: 24 Why is enzyme activity sensitive to pH?
blocks.explanation: Polypeptide chains of the enzyme are held by bonds between oppositely charged amino acids (e.g. glutamic acid – and lysine +), which are sensitive to H⁺ concentration. A pH change alters ionization of active-site amino acids and of the substrate; extreme change denatures the enzyme.

book_ref.quote: These bonds are sensitive to hydrogen ion concentration

blocks.prompt: 25 Name an enzyme that works in both acidic and alkaline media, and give its source.
blocks.explanation: Papain, obtained from green papaya, works both in acidic and alkaline media.

book_ref.quote: Some enzymes like papain from green papaya work both in acidic and alkaline media

blocks.prompt: 26 How does the rate of reaction depend on enzyme concentration when substrate is unlimited?
blocks.explanation: The rate depends directly on the amount of enzyme present. More enzyme molecules give more active sites, so more substrate is bound and transformed into products.

book_ref.quote: The overall rate of enzyme-controlled reactions depends directly on the amount of enzyme present

blocks.prompt: 27 Why does the rate of reaction stop rising when enzyme concentration increases but substrate stays the same?
blocks.explanation: Because all the available substrate is already bound; no more substrate molecules are left to attach with the extra enzymes, so the rate stays constant.

book_ref.quote: no more substrate molecules will attach with enzymes

blocks.prompt: 28 Differentiate between the effect of substrate concentration at low and high levels (enzyme constant).
blocks.explanation: With enzyme concentration kept constant:

book_ref.quote: a point is reached where any further increase in substrate does not increase the rate of reaction any more

rows: Enzyme molecules have free active sites
All active sites are occupied
New substrate binds free sites; more product per unit time
Extra substrate finds no free sites
Rate of reaction increases
Rate of reaction does not increase any more

blocks.prompt: 29 What is enzyme inhibition?
blocks.explanation: A chemical (inhibitor) attaches with the enzyme but is not transformed into products, so it blocks the active sites temporarily or permanently. This phenomenon is enzyme inhibition.

book_ref.quote: Inhibitors attach with enzymes but are not transformed into products

blocks.prompt: 30 How does aspirin suppress pain and inflammation?
blocks.explanation: Aspirin is an enzyme inhibitor used as a drug. It inhibits the enzymes that produce prostaglandin, which causes inflammation; so pain and inflammation are suppressed.

book_ref.quote: Thus, aspirin suppresses pain and inflammation

blocks.prompt: 31 Why is cyanide a poison?
blocks.explanation: Cyanide is an irreversible enzyme inhibitor. It combines with copper and iron in the active site of cytochrome oxidase and blocks cellular respiration.

book_ref.quote: The poison cyanide is an irreversible enzyme inhibitor

blocks.prompt: 32 Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive inhibitors on the basis of their site of binding.
blocks.explanation: They bind at different places on the enzyme:

book_ref.quote: Its binding alters the shape of enzyme so that active site does not fit substrate

rows: Resembles the substrate
No real structural similarity to the substrate
Binds at the active site, competing with the substrate
Does not enter the active site; binds elsewhere
Blocks the active site so substrate cannot attach
Alters the enzyme's shape so the active site does not fit the substrate

blocks.prompt: 33 Explain the competitive inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase by malonic acid.
blocks.explanation: Succinic dehydrogenase oxidizes succinic acid to fumaric acid. Malonic acid is structurally similar to succinic acid, so both compete for the active site; when malonic acid is selected, it blocks the active site.

book_ref.quote: So, both of them compete for active site of enzyme

blocks.prompt: 34 How is succinyl-CoA synthetase inhibited by its own product?
blocks.explanation: Succinic acid and CoA react to form succinyl-CoA, catalysed by succinyl-CoA synthetase. The product succinyl-CoA binds the enzyme as a non-competitive inhibitor, so no more succinyl-CoA is produced.

book_ref.quote: This reaction is catalysed by enzyme succinyl-CoA synthetase

blocks.prompt: 35 How do some antibiotics act as competitive inhibitors?
blocks.explanation: Their molecules are similar in structure to the substrates of bacterial enzymes necessary for the bacteria's life. So they bind to and block the active sites of those enzymes, killing the bacteria. (Book correction: they resemble the substrates, not the enzymes.)

book_ref.quote: These antibiotic molecules are similar in structure to the substrates of bacterial enzymes

blocks.prompt: 36 Differentiate between reversible and irreversible inhibitors.
blocks.explanation: They differ in the bond formed with the enzyme:

book_ref.quote: depending upon the kind of bond formed between inhibitor and enzyme

rows: Make covalent bonds with the enzyme
Make weak bonds (e.g. hydrogen bonds)
Not released by dilution, dialysis or more substrate
Can be released; inhibition neutralized by increasing substrate
Example: penicillin
Example: malonate

blocks.prompt: 37 How does malonate slow down cellular respiration?
blocks.explanation: Malonate is a reversible inhibitor; it temporarily blocks the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, involved in cellular respiration. The inhibition is reversed when malonate is removed.

book_ref.quote: This inhibition can be reversed when malonate is removed

blocks.prompt: 38 Why does a metabolic pathway need to be shut down? How is it done?
blocks.explanation: To regulate the concentration of the desired end product. It is done by feedback inhibition: the final product reacts with an initial enzyme and changes its conformation, so that enzyme cannot bind its substrate and the pathway closes.

book_ref.quote: In order to regulate the concentration of that product, pathway needs to be shut down

blocks.prompt: 39 Give an example of feedback inhibition involving ATP.
blocks.explanation: When a cell has more ATP than it needs, ATP itself acts as a non-competitive inhibitor and blocks the enzyme that catalyses ATP synthesis.

book_ref.quote: blocks the enzyme that catalyses ATP synthesis

blocks.prompt: 40 Give two medical uses of enzyme inhibitors.
blocks.explanation:
1. Many drugs are inhibitors: antibiotics inhibit bacterial enzymes and cancer drugs may inhibit enzymes of cell division.
2. Inhibitors of blood-clotting enzymes are used as anticoagulants. (Knowing how toxins inhibit enzymes also helps in treating poisoning.)

book_ref.quote: Some toxins and poisons inhibit important enzymes in the body

blocks.prompt: 41 How are enzyme inhibitors useful in research?
blocks.explanation: They are valuable tools in pharmaceutical research, used to study the function of specific enzymes and potential drugs. Inhibition is also an important part of studying enzyme kinetics.

book_ref.quote: Enzyme inhibitors serve as valuable tools in pharmaceutical research

blocks.prompt: 42 What are oxidoreductases? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Oxidoreductases catalyse oxidation/reduction of their substrates by adding or removing H⁺ ions or electrons. Example: cytochrome oxidase catalyses the oxidation of cytochrome.

book_ref.quote: They add or remove H⁺ ions or electrons from substrates

blocks.prompt: 43 Differentiate between transferases and lyases.
blocks.explanation: Both deal with groups, but differently:

book_ref.quote: These enzymes catalyse non-hydrolytic addition or removal of groups

rows: Transfer a functional group (methyl, acyl, amino, phosphate) from one substrate to another
Non-hydrolytic addition or removal of groups (e.g. CO₂, NH₂) from substrates
Example: hexokinase transfers phosphate from ATP to glucose
Example: pyruvate decarboxylase removes CO₂ from pyruvic acid

blocks.prompt: 44 What are isomerases? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Isomerases catalyse intra-molecular rearrangement, converting one isomer into another. Example: hexose isomerase converts glucose to fructose.

book_ref.quote: These enzymes catalyse the intra-molecular rearrangement

blocks.prompt: 45 What are proteases? Name two.
blocks.explanation: Proteases catalyse the breakdown of proteins. Examples: pepsin and trypsin (break large polypeptides into smaller ones) and erepsin (breaks dipeptides into amino acids).

book_ref.quote: This group included the enzymes which catalyse the breakdown of proteins

blocks.prompt: 46 Differentiate between maltase and sucrase.
blocks.explanation: Both are carbohydrases acting on disaccharides:

book_ref.quote: These enzymes act upon bigger carbohydrates and break them into smaller units

rows: Acts on maltose
Acts on sucrose
Product: glucose
Products: glucose and fructose

blocks.prompt: 47 What are lipases? Give an example with its products.
blocks.explanation: Lipases act upon lipids and catalyse their breakdown. Example: pancreatic lipase hydrolyses lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

book_ref.quote: These enzymes act upon lipids and catalyse their breakdown

blocks.prompt: 48 What are carbohydrases? Give the action of amylase and cellulase.
blocks.explanation: Carbohydrases act upon bigger carbohydrates and break them into smaller units. Amylase breaks starch or glycogen into maltose; cellulase breaks cellulose into cellobiose (a disaccharide) or glucose.

book_ref.quote: Cellulase breaks cellulose into cellobiose

blocks.prompt: 49 What are ligases? Which bonds do they form?
blocks.explanation: Ligases catalyse reactions in which two molecules join by forming new C–C, C–N, C–O or C–S bonds, using energy from ATP.

book_ref.quote: These enzymes catalyse the reactions in which two molecules join
